title: South Africa | FIC Act Compliance: RMCP, Reporting and Training
tagline: Master South Africa's FIC Act: your bank's RMCP, CDD and PEPs, CTRs and STRs, UN sanctions, records and what the PA enforces.
sectors: South African banks and mutual banks
AML compliance and financial crime teams
description:
A South Africa-specific anti-money laundering, counter-terrorist financing and counter-proliferation financing quest for bank staff. It is based on the **Financial Intelligence Centre Act 38 of 2001** as amended in **2008**, **2017** (Act 1 of 2017) and **2022** (the General Laws Amendment Act 22 of 2022 and the POCDATARA Amendment Act 23 of 2022), the **Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing Control Regulations**, and the supervisory practice of the **Prudential Authority** of the South African Reserve Bank, with reports going to the **Financial Intelligence Centre**.

Section 43 of the FIC Act requires banks to give employees **ongoing training** so they can comply with the Act and their bank's Risk Management and Compliance Programme, and s 62 makes failure to train sanctionable. This quest is for frontline, operations, compliance and management staff who apply CDD, report to the FIC, screen against UN sanctions or oversee the programme, at a time when South Africa has just left the FATF grey list and faces a new mutual evaluation.

It builds knowledge of the law and real PA enforcement; it does not replace your institution's own RMCP, policies and procedures, which you must always follow.
audience: Branch, teller and contact-centre staff in South African banks who handle cash and open accounts
Onboarding, KYC and relationship staff applying CDD, beneficial ownership and PEP rules
Transaction monitoring, reporting and sanctions screening analysts
Trade finance, payments and correspondent banking staff exposed to TFS and proliferation financing risk
Compliance officers, senior managers and directors responsible for the RMCP under s 42A
outcomes: Explain the FIC Act framework, its 2017 and 2022 amendments and the roles of the FIC and the Prudential Authority
Describe what a section 42 RMCP must contain and how it is approved, reviewed and made available
Apply CDD, beneficial ownership, PEP and prominent influential person rules under ss 20A to 21H
Make and escalate cash threshold and suspicious reports on time without tipping off
Apply UN targeted financial sanctions under ss 26A to 28A and recognise proliferation financing
Explain governance, training, record keeping and the s 45C sanctions regime using real PA cases

quest.name: The Kestrel Inspection
quest.premise: You have just joined the AML compliance team of Kestrel Bank Limited, a South African bank headquartered in Sandton with hubs in Cape Town and Durban. South Africa has left the FATF grey list, a new mutual evaluation is coming, and the Prudential Authority has booked an on-site FIC Act inspection. With Head of AML Compliance Thandiwe Mokoena, branch manager Pieter van der Merwe, sanctions analyst Ayesha Patel, relationship manager Sipho Ndlovu and risk committee chair Nomvula Dlamini, clear five stages, then face the inspector's questions.

sessions.title: The FIC Act, the Risk-Based Approach and the RMCP
sessions.summary: Map South Africa's AML/CFT/CPF regime: the FIC Act and its 2008, 2017 and 2022 amendments, the roles of the FIC and the Prudential Authority, the grey-list journey and the section 42 Risk Management and Compliance Programme.
objectives: Explain how the FIC Act and its 2008, 2017 and 2022 amendments fit together
Distinguish the roles of the FIC, the Prudential Authority and the bank's board
Describe what section 42 requires of a Risk Management and Compliance Programme
Explain why the 2025 grey-list exit raises, not lowers, the bar for effectiveness

cards.title: Day one at Kestrel Bank
cards.setting: AML Compliance floor, Kestrel Bank Limited head office, Sandton. Monday, 8:15 am.

lines.text: Your access card still smells of new plastic when Thandiwe Mokoena, Head of AML Compliance, waves you into a glass meeting room.
Welcome to Kestrel. South Africa came off the FATF grey list in October 2025, and the next mutual evaluation is already being prepared. The assessors will test whether our controls actually work.
And the Prudential Authority is booked for an on-site FIC Act inspection next quarter. I need you to know the Act well enough to explain it to anyone in this bank.
Thandi, Pieter here from the Durban branch. Head office sent us a new policy pack, but my tellers keep asking if the old 'internal rules' still apply. Which document actually counts?
Same question from business banking in Cape Town. We onboard trading companies every week. Are we following a rulebook or making risk calls?
Both, in a sense, and that is Stage 1 of your quest. Find out what the FIC Act asks of an accountable institution, and why our Risk Management and Compliance Programme sits at the centre of it.

scenes.heading: The FIC Act
scenes.narration: The Financial Intelligence Centre Act of 2001 is the backbone. It lists accountable institutions, banks included, and tells them how to know their clients, keep records, report to the Centre and manage risk.

scenes.heading: Three big rewrites
scenes.narration: Amendments in 2008 created administrative sanctions. The 2017 amendment moved banks from fixed internal rules to a risk-based programme. The 2022 General Laws amendments added proliferation financing, renamed PEPs and tightened beneficial ownership.

scenes.heading: The Financial Intelligence Centre
scenes.narration: The FIC is South Africa's financial intelligence unit. It receives cash threshold, suspicious activity and sanctions-related reports, analyses them and shares intelligence with law enforcement.

scenes.heading: The Prudential Authority
scenes.narration: For banks, the Prudential Authority inside the South African Reserve Bank is the FIC Act supervisory body. It inspects banks, assesses their programmes and imposes administrative sanctions when they fall short.

scenes.heading: Your bank's RMCP
scenes.narration: Every accountable institution must build, document, maintain and implement a Risk Management and Compliance Programme. Almost every duty in the Act is carried out 'in accordance with' that programme.

cards.title: How the FIC Act regime grew
cards.caption: Dates from the gazetted Acts and the National Treasury statement of 24 October 2025. Commencement of the 2022 amendments was phased.

items.label: FIC Act enacted
items.detail: Act 38 of 2001 creates the Centre, accountable institutions and reporting duties.

items.label: Sanctions added
items.detail: Act 11 of 2008 lets the Centre and supervisors impose administrative sanctions.

items.label: Risk-based approach
items.detail: Act 1 of 2017 brings in the RMCP, beneficial ownership, PEP rules and UN financial sanctions.

items.label: General Laws amendments
items.detail: Acts 22 and 23 of 2022 add proliferation financing, PEP renaming and new designation routes.

items.label: Grey-listed
items.detail: FATF places South Africa under increased monitoring with an action plan.

items.label: Grey-list exit
items.detail: FATF confirms South Africa has completed its action plan.

cards.title: Who does what?
cards.prompt: Match each body or document to its role in South Africa's regime.

pairs.right: Receives reports from accountable institutions and analyses financial intelligence
Supervises banks' FIC Act compliance, inspects them and imposes sanctions
Must ensure the bank and its staff comply with the Act and the RMCP
Assists the board, led by a person with enough competence and seniority
The bank's documented programme for managing ML, TF and PF risk
Announced the grey-list exit and coordinates the national AML/CFT effort

cards.question: Since the 2017 amendments, what does section 42 of the FIC Act require a bank to develop, document, maintain and implement?
options: A set of internal rules prescribed word for word by the FIC
A Risk Management and Compliance Programme for ML, TF and (since 2022) PF risk
A licence application to the Prudential Authority for each new product
A single annual report on all suspicious transactions
cards.explanation: The 2017 substitution of s 42 replaced 'internal rules' with a Risk Management and Compliance Programme, and the 2022 amendments extended it to proliferation financing risk.

cards.title: From rulebook to risk-based programme
The s 42(2)(a) risk cycle
cards.caption: Section 42(2)(a) lists these five verbs. Supervisors look for the reasoning behind each step, not just the result.

items.label: Identify
items.detail: Which products, clients, channels and places expose the bank to ML, TF or PF?

items.label: Assess
items.detail: Rate inherent risk, with a written rationale for each rating.

items.label: Monitor
items.detail: Watch transactions and risk indicators over time.

items.label: Mitigate
items.detail: Apply controls: EDD, limits, approvals, monitoring rules.

items.label: Manage
items.detail: Govern residual risk, update the RMCP and report to the board.

cards.title: Is it really in section 42?
cards.prompt: Sort each statement: is it a requirement of s 42, or a myth?

items.text: The board or senior management must approve the RMCP
The RMCP must be reviewed at regular intervals
Staff who handle covered transactions must have access to the RMCP documentation
If a s 42(2) item does not apply, the RMCP must say so and give the reason
The RMCP must cover proliferation financing risk
The Prudential Authority must approve the RMCP before it is used
A bank may adopt the FIC's template RMCP unchanged and be compliant
Only the compliance team needs to see the RMCP

cards.title: The trade finance rating
cards.setting: Video call between Sandton and the Cape Town business banking hub, Tuesday afternoon.

lines.text: Quick one before the inspection. Our risk assessment rates trade finance as 'medium' inherent risk. We have a lot of import advance payments to new suppliers.
Who decided 'medium', and where is the reasoning written down?
Honestly? It was copied from last year's sheet. I think somebody chose it in a workshop.
Nomvula Dlamini, chair of the board risk committee. I approved that RMCP in good faith. If the rating has no rationale, the board approved a guess.
The PA has already sanctioned a bank over exactly this kind of gap. So what do we do before the inspectors arrive?

cards.title: Fixing the unexplained rating
cards.situation: Kestrel's RMCP rates trade finance as medium inherent risk, with no documented rationale and no confirmed residual rating. The inspection is in eight weeks. Thandiwe asks you to recommend the next step.

choices.text: Re-run the assessment for trade finance with documented risk factors, set a reasoned inherent and residual rating, and take the updated RMCP to the board for approval
choices.outcome: Best. Section 42 expects the bank to identify and assess risk with reasons, and s 42(2B) expects the approving body to sign off what changes. You leave an audit trail the PA can follow.

choices.text: Change the rating to 'high' everywhere so nobody can say the bank under-rated it
choices.outcome: Partly right: a cautious rating is safer than an unexplained one, but a rating with no rationale is still a guess, and over-rating everything wastes EDD effort on low-risk clients.

choices.text: Leave the rating alone and brief staff to say it reflects management judgement
choices.outcome: Poor. Without documented reasoning, the bank cannot show it identified and assessed the risk. 'Management judgement' with no record is what the PA criticised in real sanction notices.

choices.text: Ask the PA to approve the rating in advance so the bank is protected
choices.outcome: Poor. The PA states that it does not formally approve RMCPs. Ownership of the risk assessment stays with the bank and its board.

cards.title: Real case: HBZ Bank Limited (PA, 2025)
cards.body:
In a media release dated **20 June 2025**, the Prudential Authority announced sanctions on **HBZ Bank Limited** after a 2022 FIC Act inspection: three cautions, two reprimands and a financial penalty of **R9 million**, of which R1.5 million was conditionally suspended.

Among the s 42 findings, the bank could not show:
- a **documented rationale** for rating trade finance as 'medium' inherent risk for its business model;
- a precise or confirmed **residual** risk rating for trade finance;
- that it had **implemented its RMCP** on several advance payment transactions and on CDD and record keeping.

The PA also found CDD and EDD gaps on sampled medium- and high-risk client files.

**Lesson:** a risk rating is only as good as the reasoning you can show. Writing the RMCP is half the job; proving it runs is the other half.

items.detail: FATF placed South Africa under increased monitoring.

items.label: Action items

cards.back: A business listed in Schedule 1 to the FIC Act, banks included, that must carry out CDD, keep records, report and run an RMCP.
The regulator that supervises an accountable institution's FIC Act compliance. For banks, the Prudential Authority.
An ongoing arrangement with a client versus a one-off transaction. The Act applies CDD to both, with extra steps for relationships.
Risk Management and Compliance Programme: the bank's documented, board-approved and regularly reviewed AML/CFT/CPF programme under s 42.
Providing property, services or economic support to a non-State actor that may be used to finance weapons of mass destruction or their delivery.
Matching the depth of controls to the assessed risk, with documented reasons, instead of applying one fixed set of steps to everyone.

cards.question: Pieter's tellers ask whether they need to read the RMCP, since 'it's a compliance document'. What does the FIC Act say?
options: Only managers need access; tellers follow verbal instructions
The RMCP is confidential to the board and the Prudential Authority
Documentation describing the RMCP must be available to each employee involved in transactions the Act covers
Tellers only need it if the bank has been sanctioned before
cards.explanation: Section 42(3) requires the bank to make RMCP documentation available to every employee involved in covered transactions, and s 43 requires training on the parts that apply to them.

cards.title: Stage 1 take-aways
items: The FIC Act (as amended in 2008, 2017 and 2022) sets the duties; the FIC receives reports and the PA supervises banks.
Section 42 requires a documented RMCP covering ML, TF and PF risk: identify, assess, monitor, mitigate and manage.
The board or senior management approves the RMCP, it is reviewed regularly, and staff who handle covered transactions can see it.
The PA does not approve RMCPs; it inspects whether they are reasoned and actually implemented.
South Africa exited the FATF grey list on 24 October 2025, and the next mutual evaluation will test effectiveness.

cards.prompt: Think about one product or channel you work with. Could you explain to an inspector why your bank rates its risk the way it does, and where that reasoning is written down?

quiz.question: Which body supervises South African banks' compliance with the FIC Act and can impose administrative sanctions on them?
options: The Financial Intelligence Centre's analysis unit alone
The National Prosecuting Authority's asset forfeiture unit
The Prudential Authority within the South African Reserve Bank
The Financial Sector Conduct Authority's banking ombud office
quiz.explanation: The PA is the FIC Act supervisory body for banks and imposes sanctions under s 45C. The FIC receives and analyses reports; it is not the bank supervisor.

quiz.question: Kestrel's new compliance manager wants to keep the bank's pre-2017 'internal rules' and rename them RMCP. What is the main legal problem?
options: The RMCP must be built on the bank's own assessment of ML, TF and PF risk, not on fixed prescribed steps
Internal rules are still required alongside the RMCP, so renaming them removes a document
The RMCP must be submitted to the FIC for registration before it can be used
Internal rules cannot be reused because the 2017 Act made them a criminal offence
quiz.explanation: The 2017 substitution of s 42 replaced internal rules with a programme that identifies, assesses, monitors, mitigates and manages risk. A renamed rulebook without a risk assessment misses the point.

quiz.question: Under s 42(2A), what must a bank do if one of the items listed in s 42(2) does not apply to its business?
options: Ask the PA for a written exemption before omitting the item
Leave the item out without comment because silence implies it is not relevant
Copy the item into the RMCP anyway and mark it for future use
State in the RMCP that the item does not apply and give the reason
quiz.explanation: Section 42(2A) requires the RMCP to indicate any paragraph that is not applicable and explain why. No prior exemption is needed.

quiz.question: Which statement about RMCP approval is correct?
options: The Prudential Authority must approve it before implementation
The board, senior management or the highest authority in the bank must approve it
The Financial Intelligence Centre approves it as part of registration
The external auditor approves it in the annual audit opinion
quiz.explanation: Section 42(2B) puts approval on the board, senior management or the highest level of authority. The PA has stated that it does not formally approve RMCPs.

quiz.question: Since the 2022 General Laws amendments, which risks must the RMCP enable a bank to identify, assess, monitor, mitigate and manage?
options: Money laundering and terrorist financing only
Money laundering, terrorist financing and proliferation financing
Money laundering, fraud and cybercrime
Terrorist financing and sanctions evasion only
quiz.explanation: Section 39 of the 2022 Act amended s 42(1) and (2)(a) to add proliferation financing to the programme.

quiz.question: Nomvula, the risk committee chair, asks whether South Africa's grey-list exit means supervision will ease. What is the best answer?
options: Yes; banks are exempt from inspections for three years after an exit
Yes; the action plan items fall away once the country leaves the list
No; the next FATF mutual evaluation will test whether controls work in practice
No; the country remains on the grey list until the next evaluation ends
quiz.explanation: National Treasury said the exit is the start of a broader process and that the next mutual evaluation is expected to run from 2026 to October 2027, focusing on effectiveness.

quiz.question: An inspector asks Sipho why trade finance is rated 'medium'. He says it was carried over from last year. Which real PA finding does this most closely mirror?
options: HBZ Bank, which could not evidence a documented rationale for its trade finance rating
Bank of Taiwan, which was fined for late cash threshold reports
Standard Bank, which was sanctioned for having no RMCP at all
Capitec, which was sanctioned only for sanctions screening failures
quiz.explanation: The PA's June 2025 notice on HBZ Bank cited the lack of a documented rationale for rating trade finance as medium inherent risk. The other options misstate those cases.

quiz.question: How often must a bank review its RMCP under the FIC Act?
options: Only when the Prudential Authority issues a directive to do so
Once every five years, in line with record-keeping periods
Only after the bank has filed a suspicious transaction report
At regular intervals, so it stays relevant to the bank's operations
quiz.explanation: Section 42(2C) requires review at regular intervals. The bank sets the interval in its governance framework and must evidence that reviews happen.

quiz.question: Pieter's branch manual says tellers may skip RMCP training because they 'only take deposits'. Which provisions does this conflict with most directly?
options: Sections 26A and 26B: the UN financial sanctions prohibitions
Section 28A: reporting property of designated persons
Sections 42(3) and 43: RMCP access and ongoing training for staff in covered transactions
Section 45D: appeals against administrative sanctions
quiz.explanation: Tellers handle transactions covered by the Act, so s 42(3) gives them access to the RMCP and s 43 requires ongoing training on the parts that apply to them.

quiz.question: The Bank of Taiwan, South Africa Branch was sanctioned in 2025 partly because it could not show that RMCP amendments were approved before use. Which subsection did that engage?
options: Section 42(2B), approval by the highest level of authority
Section 42(4), giving the FIC a copy on request
Section 29(3), the bar on disclosing a report
Section 23(b), keeping transaction records for five years
quiz.explanation: Approval of the RMCP by the board, senior management or highest authority is the s 42(2B) duty. The PA notice cited missing evidence of executive committee approval.

sessions.title: Customer Due Diligence, Beneficial Ownership, PEPs and PIPs
sessions.summary: Apply sections 20A to 21H: identification and verification, the business relationship profile, beneficial ownership of companies and trusts, ongoing due diligence, and the 2022 rules for politically exposed and prominent influential persons.
objectives: Apply the CDD steps in ss 20A to 21C under the bank's RMCP
Identify beneficial owners of companies, partnerships and trusts using the s 21B cascade
Distinguish foreign PEPs, domestic PEPs and prominent influential persons after the 2022 amendments
Decide what to do when CDD cannot be completed or earlier information is doubtful

cards.title: The trust with three layers
cards.setting: Business banking hub, Kestrel Bank, Cape Town. Wednesday, 10:30 am.

lines.text: New client: Bluegum Logistics (Pty) Ltd. It wants a transactional account and a trade facility. Fifty-five percent is held by a family trust, and the rest by a Mauritius company.
The trust's trustee is another company. The director signing the forms says 'the family' owns it. Is the director enough for our records?
Not even close. The Act wants the natural people behind every layer: who owns, who controls, and who benefits.
Ayesha from sanctions and screening. One more thing: the director's brother-in-law was a cabinet minister in another country until 2021. Our old procedure said PEP status lapses after twelve months.
That changed in 2022. So, Stage 2: how deep do we dig, and what extra steps does a politically exposed person trigger?

cards.title: Customer due diligence under the FIC Act

scenes.heading: No anonymous clients
scenes.narration: Section 20A bars a bank from dealing with an anonymous client or one using an apparently false or fictitious name. Everything else builds on that.

scenes.heading: Identify and verify
scenes.narration: Section 21 requires the bank, following its RMCP, to establish and verify the client's identity, and the identity and authority of anyone acting for the client or for whom the client acts.

scenes.heading: Understand the relationship
scenes.narration: Section 21A adds the nature and intended purpose of a business relationship and the source of the funds the client expects to use, so future transactions can be judged against that profile.

scenes.heading: Look through entities
scenes.narration: Section 21B requires, for companies, partnerships and trusts, the nature of the business, the ownership and control structure, and the identity of each beneficial owner.

scenes.heading: Keep it current
scenes.narration: Section 21C requires ongoing due diligence: monitoring transactions, checking source of funds where needed, and keeping client information up to date.

cards.title: Finding the beneficial owner of a company (s 21B(2))
cards.caption: The 2022 amendments added that control by other means includes control through ownership or control of other legal persons, partnerships or trusts.

items.label: Controlling ownership
items.detail: Identify each natural person who, alone or with others, has a controlling ownership interest.

items.label: Control by other means
items.detail: If in doubt or nobody qualifies, identify who controls the company by other means, including through other entities.

items.label: Control of management
items.detail: If still nobody, identify who controls management: executive officers, directors or managers.

items.label: Reasonable verification
items.detail: Take reasonable steps to verify the identity so the bank is satisfied it knows who the beneficial owner is.

cards.title: Onboarding a trust client
cards.prompt: Put the s 21B(4) steps for a trust in a sensible working order.
steps: Record the trust's name and number and the Master's office where it is registered
Identify each founder, and the beneficial owner if a founder is an entity
Identify each trustee and anyone authorised to act for the trust
Identify named beneficiaries, or record how beneficiaries are determined
Take reasonable steps to verify the particulars and identities obtained

cards.question: Bluegum's director says the trust is 'the family'. Under the 2022 definition, who is a beneficial owner?
options: Any person who signs the account mandate
A natural person who directly or indirectly ultimately owns or effectively controls the client
The company that holds the largest block of shares
Only shareholders with at least 25 percent of the shares
cards.explanation: The 2022 definition looks through to natural persons who ultimately own or effectively control the client, directly or via other entities. The Act itself sets no 25 percent figure; the RMCP explains how the bank applies 'controlling ownership interest'.

cards.title: PEPs and PIPs after 2022
cards.body:
The 2022 General Laws amendments renamed and reshaped the categories:

| Category | Who | What the bank must do |
|---|---|---|
| **Foreign PEP** (s 21F, Sch 3B) | Holds or **has held** a prominent public function in a foreign country | Always: senior management approval, reasonable measures on source of wealth and funds, enhanced ongoing monitoring |
| **Domestic PEP** (s 21G, Sch 3A) | Holds (including acting for more than six months) or **has held** a prominent public function in South Africa, or heads an international organisation | The same measures **if** the RMCP assessment shows higher risk |
| **Prominent influential person** (s 21G, Sch 3C) | Within the last 12 months, board chair, audit committee chair, executive officer or CFO of a company supplying an organ of state above a value set by the Minister | The same measures **if** higher risk |

The old 12-month cut-off was **removed** for foreign and domestic PEPs. Section 21H extends these rules to **immediate family members** and **known close associates**.

cards.title: Always, or only if higher risk?
cards.prompt: Under ss 21F-21G, do the enhanced PEP measures apply automatically, or only where the RMCP finds higher risk?

items.text: A former foreign head of state opening a private banking account
The spouse of a serving foreign government minister
A known close business associate of a senior foreign army general
A serving South African provincial premier
The chief financial officer of a company supplying a state department above the Minister's value
The adult child of a South African cabinet minister
The head of an international organisation acting in that role for over six months

cards.title: Twelve months is not a shield

lines.text: I've confirmed it. The brother-in-law served as a cabinet minister in another country until 2021, so he is a foreign PEP. Under the old wording he would have dropped off after a year.
But he's not even the client. He's related to the director, and the director isn't a beneficial owner.

Then we need to know whether he has any ownership or control in Bluegum or the trust. If he's a beneficiary of that trust, he may be a beneficial owner, and foreign PEP rules apply to him and his relatives.
The trust deed names three beneficiaries. One of them is his wife.

cards.title: A foreign PEP connection
cards.situation: Ayesha finds that a named beneficiary of Bluegum's controlling trust is the wife of a former foreign cabinet minister. The relationship manager wants to open the account today to meet a supplier deadline. What should happen?

choices.text: Treat the beneficiary as a family member of a foreign PEP: get senior management approval, take reasonable measures on source of wealth and funds, and set enhanced monitoring before opening
choices.outcome: Best. A named trust beneficiary is part of the beneficial ownership picture, and s 21H applies foreign PEP measures to immediate family members. Foreign PEP measures under s 21F are not optional.

choices.text: Open the account now and complete PEP checks within the first month of activity
choices.outcome: Poor. Section 21F requires senior management approval for establishing the relationship, so the approval comes first, not after the account is live.

choices.text: Apply the measures only if the bank's risk model rates Bluegum as high risk overall
choices.outcome: Partly right: that test is how domestic PEPs and PIPs work under s 21G. For a foreign PEP connection, s 21F applies the measures without a separate higher-risk finding.

choices.text: Decline the client automatically because PEP-linked relationships are prohibited
choices.outcome: Poor. The Act does not prohibit PEP relationships; it requires enhanced measures. Declining may be a business decision, but it is not what the law demands.

cards.title: Inability to do CDD (s 21E) vs doubts about information (s 21D)
headers: s 21D: doubts or after a report

items.label: Trigger
items.left: Bank cannot identify, verify, obtain s 21A information or do ongoing due diligence
items.right: Bank doubts earlier information, or has made a s 29 report

items.label: What the Act requires
items.left: Do not open or transact; terminate an existing relationship per the RMCP
items.right: Repeat the s 21 and s 21B steps as far as needed to confirm

items.label: Reporting
items.right: If triggered by a report, update CDD carefully to avoid tipping off

cards.title: Real case: Capitec Bank Limited (PA, 2024)
Real case: State Bank of India, South Africa (PA, 2024)
cards.body:
On **2 August 2024** the SARB announced sanctions on the **State Bank of India, South Africa** after a FIC Act inspection in May 2020: four cautions and penalties totalling **R10 million**, with R4.5 million conditionally suspended for 36 months.

The first finding was a failure to conduct **basic and enhanced due diligence** on sampled client files under ss 21(1) and 21A, which carried a R5 million penalty (R3 million suspended). Other findings covered cash threshold reporting, the risk assessment and RMCP, and governance under s 42A.

The PA stressed that the sanctions were **not** because the bank was involved in laundering or terrorist financing.

**Lesson:** you can be sanctioned for weak controls even when no criminal money is proven to have passed through.

cards.back: Where the money for a transaction or relationship comes from, such as salary, sale proceeds or trade receipts.
How the client built their overall wealth over time. Required by reasonable measures for PEPs under ss 21F-21G.
Someone with a close business or personal link to a PEP or PIP. Section 21H applies PEP measures to them.
Lighter measures the RMCP may permit for lower-risk relationships under s 42(2)(m), with reasons.
Extra measures the RMCP sets for higher-risk single transactions and relationships under s 42(2)(m).

cards.question: Sipho cannot verify who controls Bluegum's Mauritius shareholder, and the client refuses to explain. What does s 21E require?
options: Open the account but flag it for review in six months
Do not establish the relationship, and consider making a s 29 report
Open the account if the trust's beneficiaries have been verified
Ask the FIC for permission to proceed without the information
cards.explanation: Section 21E bars establishing the relationship or transacting when CDD cannot be completed, and tells the bank to consider a s 29 report.

cards.title: Stage 2 take-aways
items: Sections 20A-21C: no anonymous clients; identify and verify; understand purpose, nature and source of funds; look through entities; keep CDD current.
Beneficial owners are the natural persons who ultimately own or effectively control the client, directly or through other entities.
For trusts, identify founders, trustees, authorised persons and beneficiaries, and look through any entity in those roles.
Foreign PEPs always trigger senior management approval, source of wealth and funds measures and enhanced monitoring; domestic PEPs and PIPs do when higher risk.
Since 2022 PEP status no longer lapses after 12 months; PIP status covers the preceding 12 months. Family and close associates are covered.
If CDD cannot be completed, do not proceed, terminate where needed, and consider a s 29 report.

cards.prompt: Pick a client structure you have seen with more than one layer. Could you name every natural person who owns, controls or benefits from it, and show how you verified them?

quiz.question: A walk-in customer in Durban wants to open an account using a name that does not match any document and refuses to explain. Which provision most directly prohibits proceeding?
options: Section 28, which governs cash transactions above the prescribed amount
Section 20A, which bars dealing with anonymous or apparently fictitious-name clients
Section 42A, which sets the board's duty to ensure compliance
Section 26C, which allows ministerial permission for basic expenses
quiz.explanation: Section 20A prohibits establishing a relationship or concluding a single transaction with an anonymous client or one with an apparently false or fictitious name.

quiz.question: What does s 21A add to identification and verification when a bank opens a business relationship?
options: A certified copy of the client's tax clearance certificate
A credit score from a registered credit bureau
Written consent from the FIC before the first transaction
Information on the nature and purpose of the relationship and the expected source of funds
quiz.explanation: Section 21A requires information on the nature and intended purpose of the relationship and the source of funds the client expects to use, so future activity can be compared to that profile.

quiz.question: Bluegum is 55% owned by a trust and 45% by a Mauritius company with an unclear owner. After checking ownership, nobody clearly has a controlling interest. What does s 21B(2) require next?
options: Identify who controls the company through other means, including via other entities
Record the trust as the beneficial owner and close the file
Identify only the directors listed with the companies registry
Accept a director's declaration that no beneficial owner exists
quiz.explanation: The cascade moves from controlling ownership interest to control by other means (expressly including through other legal persons, partnerships or trusts since 2022), then to control of management.

quiz.question: Which of these must a bank establish for a trust client under s 21B(4), as amended in 2022?
options: Only the trustees, because they hold legal title to trust assets
Only the beneficiaries who received a distribution in the last year
The founders, trustees and named beneficiaries, looking through any that are entities
Only the person signing on behalf of the trust and the trust's auditor
quiz.explanation: Section 21B(4) covers founders, trustees, authorised persons and beneficiaries (or how they are determined), and the 2022 amendments added the beneficial owners of any entity in those roles.

quiz.question: A former foreign finance minister left office in 2019 and now wants an investment account at Kestrel. How should the bank treat him under the amended Act?
options: As an ordinary client, since more than 12 months have passed since he left office
As a prominent influential person, since he no longer holds public office
As a domestic PEP, since the account is opened in South Africa
As a foreign PEP, since a person who has held a prominent foreign function stays covered
quiz.explanation: The 2022 amendments changed Schedule 3B so that a foreign PEP is someone who holds or has held a prominent public function abroad, removing the old 12-month limit.

quiz.question: The executive mayor of a South African municipality wants a business account. Kestrel's RMCP assessment rates the relationship as standard risk. What do ss 21G and 42(2)(l) require?
options: Apply all enhanced measures because every domestic PEP is automatically high risk
Determine PEP status under the RMCP; the enhanced measures apply only if the relationship is higher risk
Refuse the account because domestic PEPs need FIC approval
Ignore PEP status because it applies only to foreign officials
quiz.explanation: For domestic PEPs and PIPs, s 21G triggers senior management approval, source of wealth and funds measures and enhanced monitoring when the RMCP finds higher risk. Section 42(2)(l) requires the RMCP to set how status is determined.

quiz.question: Who is a prominent influential person under Schedule 3C?
options: Any senior manager of a listed company on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange
Any person who donates to a political party above a set amount
A chair, audit committee chair, executive officer or CFO of a company supplying an organ of state above a ministerially set value
A senior official of a foreign government acting in South Africa
quiz.explanation: Schedule 3C, inserted in 2022, covers those company roles (held now or in the preceding 12 months) where the company supplies goods or services to an organ of state above a value the Minister sets by notice.

quiz.question: The PA's 2024 notice on Capitec listed several CDD gaps. Which of these was among them?
options: Not obtaining senior management approval when re-rating or reviewing high-risk clients
Using a foreign currency account for a domestic PEP
Accepting electronic identity verification instead of paper copies
Refusing accounts to clients without a fixed residential address
quiz.explanation: The December 2024 notice included gaps in senior management approval for re-risk rating and high-risk reviews, alongside identity, beneficial ownership, address, source of funds and PEP screening issues.

quiz.question: Months after onboarding, Kestrel learns that a client's company registration document was forged. What does s 21D require?
options: Freeze the account and report the client to the Prudential Authority
Do nothing further, because CDD was completed at onboarding
Close the account immediately without any further steps
Repeat the s 21 and s 21B steps as far as needed to confirm the information
quiz.explanation: Section 21D requires repeating identification and verification steps to the extent needed when the bank doubts previously obtained information. Section 21E applies if the bank then cannot complete CDD.

quiz.question: A client's brother is a serving cabinet minister in a neighbouring country. The client has no other risk factors. What does s 21H mean for the bank?
options: The brother's status is irrelevant because siblings are not covered
Foreign PEP measures apply to the client as an immediate family member
Only the brother's own accounts need enhanced measures
The bank must apply simplified due diligence to offset the PEP link
quiz.explanation: Section 21H(2) lists siblings among immediate family members, so s 21F applies: senior management approval, source of wealth and funds measures and enhanced monitoring.

sessions.title: Reporting to the FIC: Cash Thresholds and Suspicion
sessions.summary: Master the section 28 cash threshold report (R49,999.99, 3 days), the section 29 suspicious and unusual report, attempted transactions, tipping off, FIC interventions and the alert-handling expectations the PA enforces.
objectives: Decide when a cash threshold report is due and by when
Recognise the grounds for a section 29 report, including structuring and attempted transactions
Handle client contact after a report without tipping off
Explain how slow alert handling turned into real PA sanctions

cards.title: Cash, cars and a queue of alerts
cards.setting: Kestrel Bank branch, Durban CBD. Thursday, 9:40 am.

lines.text: Morning rush. A used-car dealer has just deposited R62,000 in cash. Yesterday he paid in R40,000 and the day before R45,000.
My teller says we only report cash over the limit. The old system used to add up a series of deposits. Does it still?
Two separate questions there. One is the cash threshold report, which is automatic. The other is whether anyone suspects something, which is a judgement.
And there's a third problem. Monitoring has 600 alerts older than two days, and some cases from last month were never filed. The PA fined a big bank over exactly that.
Stage 3, then. By tonight you'll know which reports go to the FIC, who must make them, how fast, and what you must never say to the client.

cards.title: Reports to the Financial Intelligence Centre

scenes.heading: Cash threshold reports (s 28)
scenes.narration: When a bank pays or receives cash above the prescribed amount in a transaction with a client, it must report the prescribed particulars to the FIC. No suspicion is needed: it is a threshold test.

scenes.heading: Suspicious and unusual reports (s 29)
scenes.narration: Anyone who carries on, manages or works for a business and knows or suspects certain things about money or transactions must report the grounds to the FIC. That duty applies to employees personally.

scenes.heading: Attempted transactions count
scenes.narration: Section 29(2) covers transactions that were only enquired about. If a client walks away after asking questions that raise suspicion, the report may still be due.

scenes.heading: No tipping off
scenes.narration: A person who made or must make a report, or who knows one was made, may not disclose that or its contents, including to the client, except in limited cases the Act lists.

scenes.heading: The FIC can pause a transaction
scenes.narration: Under s 34, after consulting the bank, the FIC may direct it not to proceed with a transaction for up to 10 days, not counting weekends and public holidays, while it makes inquiries.

cards.title: Cash threshold report vs suspicious report
cards.caption: Threshold and CTR deadline from GN 2638 of 14 October 2022, effective 14 November 2022. STR period as cited in the PA's 2025 Standard Bank notice.

items.label: Trigger
items.left: Cash above R49,999.99 paid to or received from a client
items.right: Knowledge or suspicion on grounds listed in s 29

items.label: Who decides
items.left: Automatic once the amount is exceeded
items.right: Judgement by any employee, escalated per the RMCP

items.label: Deadline
items.left: As soon as possible, no later than 3 days after awareness

items.label: Linked cash
items.left: Since 14 Nov 2022 the rule no longer refers to a series of cash deals
items.right: Structuring to avoid a report is itself a s 29 ground

cards.question: The car dealer deposits R62,000 in notes today. What must Kestrel do under s 28, regardless of whether anyone is suspicious?
options: Nothing, unless the teller suspects the cash is criminal
Report the transaction to the FIC as a cash threshold report within the regulated period
Ask the PA whether the amount should be reported
Hold the cash until the dealer proves its source
cards.explanation: R62,000 exceeds the prescribed amount of R49,999.99, so a cash threshold report is due as soon as possible and no later than 3 days after the bank becomes aware. Suspicion is a separate question under s 29.

cards.title: What counts as a s 29 suspicion
cards.body:
Section 29(1) applies when a person **knows or suspects** that:
- the business has received, or is about to receive, the **proceeds of unlawful activities**;
- a transaction or series of transactions **facilitated** or is likely to facilitate the transfer of such proceeds, has **no apparent business or lawful purpose**, is conducted to **avoid a reporting duty**, may be relevant to **tax evasion**, or relates to a contravention of the **UN sanctions prohibitions** in s 26B;
- the business has been, or is about to be, **used for money laundering**.

The report gives the **grounds** for the knowledge or suspicion and the prescribed particulars.

Three practical rules:
1. You don't need proof or a named crime. Suspicion is enough.
2. The duty is **personal**. Escalating to the compliance function through the bank's internal channel is how you meet it in practice.
3. Splitting cash to stay under the threshold is **structuring**, and that is a reporting ground in its own right.

cards.title: CTR, STR, both or neither?
cards.prompt: For each event at a Kestrel branch, decide which report is due.

items.text: A supermarket deposits R80,000 in daily takings that match its known profile
A client deposits R48,000 cash three days in a row and asks how to 'avoid the paperwork'
A client asks how much cash can be paid in before the bank reports it, then leaves
A salary of R55,000 arrives by electronic transfer
A client withdraws R70,000 cash for a vehicle purchase, with matching documents
A dormant account suddenly receives many small transfers from unrelated people and pays them out in cash
A pensioner deposits R2,000 cash monthly, as for years

cards.title: Who tells the client?
cards.setting: Durban branch back office, Thursday, 2:15 pm.

lines.text: We've escalated the car dealer. Compliance filed a report. Now he's at the counter asking why his transfer to a supplier in Gaborone is 'under review'.
My teller wants to say 'compliance reported you, it's out of our hands'. Honestly, that would be easier.
Absolutely not. Section 29(3) and (4) prohibit telling him a report was made or anything about its contents.
And if updating his CDD now would alert him, s 21C(2) lets us pause that process and consider the report instead. Let's think about what the teller can say.

cards.title: At the counter
cards.situation: The car dealer demands to know why his outgoing payment is delayed. A suspicious activity report has been filed. The teller asks you what to say.

choices.text: Give a neutral answer that the payment is going through the bank's normal checks, and refer further questions to the relationship manager, without mentioning any report
choices.outcome: Best. The client gets a truthful, general response, and nothing reveals that a report was made or what it contains, which s 29(3) and (4) prohibit.

choices.text: Tell him the bank is legally obliged to report large cash deposits, so he should not worry
choices.outcome: Poor. It hints at reporting and may lead him to guess there is a suspicion. Even a well-meant hint risks tipping off.

choices.text: Ask him to come back with documents explaining all his recent cash, as the bank has concerns
choices.outcome: Partly right: asking for information can be legitimate CDD, but saying 'the bank has concerns' right after a report may alert him. Section 21C(2) allows CDD to be paused when it would disclose a report.

choices.text: Process the payment immediately so the client does not become suspicious
choices.outcome: Poor. Releasing funds to calm the client ignores the risk the report identified. The bank should follow its RMCP for post-report handling and any FIC direction under s 34.

cards.title: From alert to report
cards.prompt: Put the steps for handling a monitoring alert in a sound order.
steps: Automated monitoring raises an alert on unusual activity
An analyst reviews the alert promptly against the client's CDD profile
The analyst records written findings on the transaction's background and purpose
Unresolved suspicion is escalated to the compliance function
The report is filed with the FIC within the regulated period
CDD is refreshed under s 21D without tipping off the client

cards.title: Real case: Standard Bank of South Africa (PA, 2025)
Standard Bank sanction, January 2025
cards.caption: Figures from the PA media release of 24 January 2025.

items.label: Late STRs/SARs
items.detail: Reported after the deadline under s 29.

items.label: Slow alerts
items.detail: Not attended to within 48 hours under Directive 5 of 2019.

items.label: Late CTRs
items.detail: Cash threshold or aggregation reports filed late.

items.label: Total penalties
items.detail: Plus six cautions not to repeat the conduct.

cards.front: Myth: only compliance staff have a reporting duty
cards.back: Fact: s 29 applies to anyone who carries on, manages or is employed by a business and knows or suspects. Use the internal channel in the RMCP.

cards.front: Myth: CTRs still add up a series of cash deposits
cards.back: Fact: the 2022 regulation change deleted the words 'series of cash transactions' from the CTR rule, so each cash transaction is tested on its own.
Fact: s 29(2) covers transactions that were only enquired about and would have raised a reportable concern.

cards.front: Myth: you can tell the client once the report is filed
cards.back: Fact: s 29(3) and (4) forbid disclosing a report or its contents, before or after filing, except as the Act allows.

cards.front: Myth: alert backlogs are an operations issue, not a legal one
cards.back: Fact: the PA sanctioned banks under FIC Directive 5 of 2019 for alerts not handled within 48 hours.

cards.question: Under s 34, what can the FIC do after consulting a bank about a suspect transaction?
options: Freeze the client's account permanently without a court order
Direct the bank not to proceed with the transaction for up to 10 days, excluding weekends and public holidays
Impose an administrative penalty on the client
Order the bank to close the account and return the funds
cards.explanation: Section 34 (as amended in 2017) allows an intervention direction for up to 10 days, with weekends and public holidays excluded, so the FIC can make inquiries and inform investigators if appropriate.

cards.title: Stage 3 take-aways
items: Section 28: report cash above R49,999.99 paid to or received from a client, no later than 3 days after becoming aware (since 14 November 2022 the rule no longer covers a series of cash transactions).
Section 29: anyone in the business who knows or suspects must report the grounds, including for attempted transactions; the 15-day period is in regulation 24(3).
Structuring, no apparent lawful purpose, tax evasion and s 26B sanctions breaches are all s 29 grounds.
Never tip off: s 29(3) and (4) bar disclosing a report or its contents; s 21C(2) lets you pause CDD that would alert the client.
The FIC can stop a transaction for up to 10 working days under s 34, and slow alert handling has drawn real PA penalties.

cards.prompt: If a colleague told you about an odd transaction over lunch, would you know the exact internal channel your bank uses to turn that into a s 29 report, and how fast it must move?

quiz.question: What is the prescribed amount of cash above which a transaction must be reported under s 28, as set from 14 November 2022?
options: R25,000.00 per day in total
quiz.explanation: Government Notice 2638 of 14 October 2022 substituted regulation 22B, setting the amount at R49,999.99 with effect from 14 November 2022. The earlier figure was R24,999.99.

quiz.question: A client deposits R30,000 cash on Monday and R30,000 on Tuesday. Nothing else is unusual. Under the current regulations, is a cash threshold report due?
options: Yes, because the two deposits together exceed R49,999.99
Yes, because any cash over R25,000 must be reported within 3 days
No CTR is due, because neither deposit exceeds R49,999.99 and series reporting was removed
No, because CTRs apply only to withdrawals, not deposits
quiz.explanation: The 2022 amendment removed 'series of cash transactions' from regulation 24(4). Each transaction is tested on its own; a pattern designed to avoid reporting would instead be a s 29 matter.

quiz.question: How quickly must a s 28 cash threshold report reach the FIC under regulation 24(4) as amended in 2022?
options: Within 15 days after becoming aware of the transaction
As soon as possible, but no later than 3 days after becoming aware of the transaction
By the end of the calendar month in which it occurred
Within 48 hours of the transaction being processed
quiz.explanation: GN 2638 amended regulation 24(4) from 2 days to 3 days. The 15-day period relates to suspicious and unusual reports, and 48 hours is the Directive 5 alert-handling expectation.

quiz.question: A teller suspects a deposit is linked to fraud but her supervisor says, 'Leave it, it's a good client.' What is the teller's position under s 29?
options: The duty passes to the supervisor once she has raised it verbally
She has no duty because only the compliance officer reports to the FIC
She must contact the client first to hear an explanation
Her personal duty to report remains, so she should use the bank's internal channel to escalate
quiz.explanation: Section 29 applies to any person employed by the business who knows or suspects. Internal escalation under the RMCP is how the duty is met; a supervisor cannot cancel it, and contacting the client risks tipping off.

quiz.question: A client asks detailed questions about how much cash can be deposited 'without the bank telling anyone', then leaves without transacting. What applies?
options: Nothing applies because no transaction took place
Section 28 applies because the client mentioned a large amount
Section 29(2) can require a report even though no transaction was concluded
Section 21E applies, so the account must be closed
quiz.explanation: Section 29(2) covers transactions about which enquiries are made, if concluding them could have had the consequences in s 29(1). Avoiding a reporting duty is one of those grounds.

quiz.question: Which of these is expressly a ground for a s 29 report?
options: A transaction that relates to a contravention of the s 26B UN sanctions prohibitions
A transaction in a foreign currency that the client uses regularly
Any transfer to a country outside the Common Monetary Area
A cash deposit by a client whose account was opened more than five years ago
quiz.explanation: The 2017 amendment added s 29(1)(b)(vi), covering transactions relating to a contravention of a s 26B prohibition. The other options are not grounds on their own.

quiz.question: After a report is filed, the client asks a teller directly: 'Did you report me?' What does the law require?
options: The teller may confirm it because the client has a right to know under POPIA
The teller may confirm it once the FIC has acknowledged receipt
The teller must refer the client to the FIC to ask
The teller must not disclose that a report was made or its contents
quiz.explanation: Section 29(3) and (4) prohibit disclosing a report or its contents, including to the client, outside the listed exceptions such as legal proceedings or a court order.

quiz.question: In the January 2025 Standard Bank sanction, which finding carried the largest single penalty?
options: One suspicious transaction that was never reported to the FIC
Alerts not handled within 48 hours and alerts closed beyond the 15-day period, under FIC Directive 5 of 2019
Late cash threshold and aggregation reports under s 28
Missing ongoing due diligence reviews for two clients
quiz.explanation: The Directive 5 finding carried R8 million. The unreported STR carried R1 million, the late CTRs a caution, and the ongoing due diligence finding a caution.

quiz.question: Updating a client's CDD would require asking questions that reveal a suspicion is being reported. What does s 21C(2), added in 2022, allow?
options: The bank may stop the CDD process and consider making a s 29 report
The bank may skip both CDD and reporting until the client volunteers information
The bank must close the account immediately and inform the client why
The bank must ask the Prudential Authority for a CDD waiver
quiz.explanation: Section 21C(2) lets a bank discontinue CDD where performing it would reasonably disclose an impending report, and consider reporting under s 29 instead.

quiz.question: Who receives cash threshold and suspicious transaction reports from South African banks?
options: The Prudential Authority
The South African Police Service
The Financial Intelligence Centre
The South African Revenue Service
quiz.explanation: Reports under ss 28 and 29 go to the FIC, which analyses them and shares intelligence. The PA supervises compliance with the duty to report.

sessions.title: Targeted Financial Sanctions and Proliferation Financing
sessions.summary: Apply Part 2A of the FIC Act as amended in 2022: immediate effect of UN Security Council listings, the section 26B prohibitions, section 28A reporting and scrutiny, ministerial permissions and the new proliferation financing definition.
objectives: Explain how UN financial sanctions take effect under s 26A after 2022
Apply the s 26B prohibitions, including to persons acting for designated persons
Carry out s 28A reporting and client scrutiny after new designations
Recognise proliferation financing patterns beyond direct list matches

cards.title: A name match at 6 pm
cards.setting: Sanctions screening desk, Kestrel Bank, Sandton. Friday, 6:05 pm.

lines.text: Thandi, a payment of USD 180,000 from a Johannesburg trading company to a freight forwarder in Dubai just hit a sanctions alert. The forwarder's director is a strong match to a newly designated person.
The UN Security Council added him this afternoon, New York time. The FIC notice may not be out yet. Do we wait for it?
The client is mine. They import industrial valves and say it's urgent: a ship sails on Monday.
Industrial valves to a forwarder linked to a designated person. That could be a proliferation financing pattern, not just a sanctions hit.
Stage 4. Tonight you learn how UN sanctions take effect in South African law, what we must not do, and what we must report.

cards.title: Targeted financial sanctions in South African law

scenes.heading: One route for UN designations
scenes.narration: Part 2A of the FIC Act gives effect to UN Security Council financial sanctions. Since the 2022 amendments, terrorism designations also run through it, after the old presidential proclamation route in POCDATARA was repealed.

scenes.heading: Immediate effect
scenes.narration: Since 2022, a Chapter VII sanctions resolution has immediate effect under the Act once the Security Council adopts it. The FIC Director then publishes notice of the resolution and of the persons and entities designated.

scenes.heading: The prohibitions in section 26B
scenes.narration: No person may provide property, financial services or economic support for the benefit of a designated person, deal with their property, or help them keep or hide it. Since 2022, the rules also cover people acting for them.

scenes.heading: Report and scrutinise
scenes.narration: Section 28A requires a bank holding property of a designated person to report it to the FIC within the prescribed period, and to scrutinise its client information whenever the Director gives notice of new designations.

scenes.heading: Proliferation financing
scenes.narration: Since 2022 the Act defines proliferation financing: funds, services or support to a non-State actor that may be used for nuclear, chemical or biological weapons or their delivery systems. The RMCP must manage that risk.

cards.title: From UN listing to bank action
cards.caption: Based on ss 26A, 26B and 28A as amended by Acts 1 of 2017, 22 of 2022 and 23 of 2022.

items.label: UN adoption
items.detail: Security Council adopts or updates a Chapter VII financial sanctions resolution.

items.label: Immediate legal effect
items.detail: Under s 26A(1), the resolution takes effect for the Act upon adoption.

items.label: FIC Director's notice
items.detail: The Director publishes the resolution and designated persons and entities.

items.label: Scrutinise clients
items.detail: Banks check client information against the notice under s 28A(3).

items.label: Stop and report
items.detail: Do not deal with the property; report it to the FIC under s 28A(1).

cards.title: Part 2A and related provisions
cards.prompt: Match each provision to what it does.

pairs.right: UN Chapter VII financial sanctions take effect, and the Director gives notice of designations
Prohibits providing property, services or support to designated persons, or dealing with their property
Lets the Minister permit dealings for basic expenses and certain prior obligations
Requires reporting property of designated persons and scrutinising client information
Makes failure to comply with s 26B non-compliance subject to administrative sanction
Makes a transaction relating to a s 26B breach a ground for a suspicious report

cards.question: Ayesha asks whether the bank may release the payment because the FIC Director's notice has not been published yet. What does the amended s 26A(1) say?
options: The resolution only binds banks once a Gazette notice by the Minister appears
The resolution has immediate effect for the Act on its adoption by the Security Council
The resolution binds banks only after the PA issues a directive
The resolution applies only to persons resident in South Africa
cards.explanation: The 2022 amendment replaced the old ministerial notice step: a Chapter VII financial sanctions resolution now has immediate effect for the Act upon adoption. The Director's notice informs; it does not delay the effect.

cards.title: What the s 26B prohibitions catch
Sanctions or proliferation red flag?
cards.prompt: Sort each warning sign. Some point to a direct sanctions match, others to a wider proliferation financing pattern.

items.text: Beneficiary's name, date of birth and nationality match a newly designated person
Client's shareholder is listed in the Director's latest s 26A notice
Payment for dual-use industrial goods via a freight forwarder with no trade history
End user of high-specification valves is vague and changes between documents
Signatory on an account is the spouse of a designated person acting at their direction
Shipping route goes through several trans-shipment hubs with no commercial reason
Trade documents describe goods in unusually generic terms for the price paid

cards.title: Monday morning
cards.setting: Kestrel Bank boardroom, Sandton. Monday, 7:30 am.

lines.text: Update: the match is confirmed. The forwarder's director is the designated person. The payment is still held.
The client is furious. They say they've never met him, and their ship is sailing. Can we at least pay the freight portion?
I need to understand the board's exposure. If we release even part of it, what have we done?
We'd be providing property for the benefit of a designated person. That's a s 26B breach, and the PA can sanction it under s 49A(2). Here's what we do instead.

cards.title: The held payment
cards.situation: The beneficiary's director is confirmed as a person designated by the UN Security Council. Kestrel's client insists it did not know and asks for a partial release to cover freight costs. What should Kestrel do?

choices.text: Keep the funds blocked, report the property to the FIC under s 28A, file a s 29 report on the transaction, and tell the client only that the payment cannot be processed
choices.outcome: Best. Section 26B bars making property available for the designated person's benefit, s 28A requires reporting, and the transaction relates to a s 26B contravention, which is a s 29 ground. No tipping off.

choices.text: Release the freight portion only, since the client acted in good faith
choices.outcome: Poor. The client's good faith does not change the bank's position: releasing any part would make property available for the benefit of a designated person.

choices.text: Return the funds to the client and close the file without reporting
choices.outcome: Partly right: not paying the designated person is correct, but s 28A and s 29 reporting duties still apply, and the bank should follow its RMCP on how to handle blocked funds.

choices.text: Ask the client to apply to the bank for a basic-expenses exemption
choices.outcome: Poor. Only the Minister (or the Director under delegation) can permit dealings under s 26C. The bank cannot grant exemptions.

cards.title: Before and after the 2022 amendments
cards.caption: Earlier POCDATARA proclamations stay valid and are treated as notices under s 26A(3).

items.label: Effect of UN listings
items.left: Took effect through a Minister's notice in the Gazette
items.right: Immediate effect on adoption by the Security Council

items.label: Terrorism designations
items.right: Section 25 repealed; designations handled through FIC Act s 26A

items.label: Who is caught
items.right: Also persons acting on their behalf or at their direction

items.label: Proliferation financing
items.left: Not defined in the FIC Act
items.right: Defined; RMCP must cover PF risk

items.label: Breach of s 26B
items.right: Also non-compliance subject to administrative sanction

cards.title: Real case: screening and correspondent controls (PA, 2025)
cards.body:
The PA's **20 June 2025** sanction on the **Bank of Taiwan, South Africa Branch** shows how sanctions-related controls are judged through the RMCP. Among the s 42 findings, the branch could not show that its **Screening of Customers and Transactions Manual** had been reviewed and approved after 2020, and it had not implemented its due diligence on two **correspondent banking (vostro)** relationships.

The outcome was a caution and a reprimand, with no penalty, but the findings are public.

Why it matters for TFS:
- Screening rules must be **current**: UN lists change, and since 2022 they take effect on adoption.
- Correspondent relationships are a channel for sanctioned or proliferation-linked funds, so due diligence on them is a frontline sanctions control.
- A manual nobody has reviewed in years is a red flag to an inspector.

cards.back: A person or entity identified under a UN Security Council resolution that has effect under s 26A.
Help other than money, such as goods, logistics or services, that benefits a designated person. Covered by s 26B.
A person or entity not acting under a State's lawful authority. Part of the FIC Act's definition of proliferation financing.
Items with civilian uses that can also support weapons programmes, such as certain valves, pumps or electronics.
Written permission from the Minister (or delegated Director) allowing dealings such as basic expenses. Never granted by a bank.

cards.question: After a new s 26A notice, Kestrel's screening finds an existing client is a designated entity holding R2.3 million on deposit. Which pair of duties applies?
options: Close the account and pay the balance out to the client
Report the property to the FIC under s 28A and not deal with it under s 26B
Notify the client and give them 30 days to move the funds
Ask the client to confirm in writing that the listing is a mistake
cards.explanation: Section 28A(1) requires the bank to report property of a designated person, and s 26B prohibits dealing with it. Paying it out or warning the client would breach those duties.

cards.title: Stage 4 take-aways
items: UN Chapter VII financial sanctions have immediate effect under FIC Act s 26A on adoption; the FIC Director publishes notices.
Since 2022 terrorism designations also run through s 26A; POCDATARA's proclamation route (s 25) was repealed.
Section 26B bars anyone from giving property, services or support to designated persons, or those acting for them, or dealing with their property.
Report property of designated persons under s 28A, scrutinise clients when notices change, and file s 29 reports on related transactions.
Proliferation financing is defined in the Act, the RMCP must cover it, and only the Minister can permit exempt dealings under s 26C.

cards.prompt: When did your bank's screening lists or screening manual last change? How would you know that a UN listing adopted overnight is already being applied to your payments?

quiz.question: Since the 2022 amendments, when does a UN Security Council Chapter VII financial sanctions resolution take effect for the FIC Act?
options: When the Minister of Finance publishes a notice in the Gazette
When the Prudential Authority issues a directive to banks
Thirty days after the FIC Director publishes a notice
Immediately upon its adoption by the Security Council
quiz.explanation: Section 26A(1) as substituted in 2022 gives such a resolution immediate effect upon adoption. The Director's notice under s 26A(3) publicises it but does not delay it.

quiz.question: What happened to presidential proclamations of terrorist entities under POCDATARA s 25 in 2022?
options: They were extended to cover proliferation financing designations
Section 25 was repealed, and UN terrorism designations now run through FIC Act s 26A
They were transferred to the Prudential Authority to administer
They were kept, with the FIC Act route used only for non-terrorism lists
quiz.explanation: The POCDATARA Amendment Act 23 of 2022 repealed ss 25 and 26 and removed the s 26A(2) exclusion. Earlier proclamations remain valid as s 26A(3) notices.

quiz.question: A corporate client asks Kestrel to pay a supplier's invoice. The supplier is not designated, but Kestrel learns it acts on the direction of a designated person. What applies?
options: Nothing, because only designated persons themselves are covered
Section 28 cash threshold reporting, because the invoice is large
Section 26B, which since 2022 also covers property of persons acting on behalf of or at the direction of designated persons
Section 21G, because the supplier is a prominent influential person
quiz.explanation: The 2022 amendment to s 26B(2) extended the dealing prohibition to persons or entities acting on behalf of or at the direction of a designated person.

quiz.question: Which body or person can permit a dealing with a designated person's property for basic expenses such as food, rent and medicine?
options: The Minister, or the FIC Director acting under delegation, under s 26C
The bank's compliance officer, after documenting the reason
The Prudential Authority, through a supervisory directive
A magistrate, on application by the bank
quiz.explanation: Section 26C gives the Minister power to permit such dealings in writing, and allows delegation to the Director. Banks cannot create their own exemptions.

quiz.question: What does s 28A(3) require of a bank when the FIC Director gives notice of new designations?
options: Scrutinise its information on clients to see whether any is a designated person or entity
Suspend every account opened in the last 12 months
Send each client a copy of the notice
File a nil report with the FIC if there are no matches
quiz.explanation: Section 28A(3) requires the bank to scrutinise client information on receipt of the notice to find any designated person or entity. Nil reporting and blanket suspensions are not what it requires.

quiz.question: Which statement best matches the FIC Act definition of proliferation financing inserted in 2022?
options: Any export of military equipment without a permit from the National Conventional Arms Control Committee
Financing a State's lawful defence procurement through a South African bank
Moving funds through three or more jurisdictions to hide their origin
Providing property, services or economic support to a non-State actor that may be used for weapons of mass destruction or their delivery
quiz.explanation: The 2022 definition centres on support to a non-State actor that may finance nuclear, chemical or biological weapons and their means of delivery. The last option describes layering in money laundering.

quiz.question: What consequence did the 2022 amendments add for an accountable institution that fails to comply with s 26B?
options: Its banking licence is automatically withdrawn
It is non-compliant and subject to an administrative sanction under s 49A(2)
It must pay the designated person's frozen balance to the FIC
It loses the right to appeal any sanction to the Appeal Board
quiz.explanation: Section 49A(2), added in 2022, makes failure to comply with s 26B non-compliance subject to administrative sanction, alongside any criminal exposure.

quiz.question: Kestrel's client says it acted in good faith and asks to pay only the freight portion of a payment to a designated person's company. What is the best reason to refuse?
options: The bank cannot process partial payments under the National Payment System rules
The FIC must first approve the amount under s 34
Any part of the payment would still make property available for a designated person's benefit
Freight payments always require a separate trade licence
quiz.explanation: Section 26B prohibits providing property 'in whole or in part' for the benefit of a designated person. The client's good faith does not make the payment lawful.

quiz.question: Which of these is the strongest proliferation financing indicator in a trade payment?
options: A long-standing client paying a regular supplier in the same country
Dual-use industrial goods sent to a vague end user through unexplained trans-shipment points
An invoice paid in US dollars rather than rand
A client using a letter of credit instead of open account terms
quiz.explanation: Proliferation networks often use dual-use goods, unclear end users and indirect routes. Currency or payment method alone is not an indicator.

quiz.question: The PA's 2025 notice on the Bank of Taiwan, South Africa Branch included which sanctions-related control finding?
options: Failure to report a designated person's account under s 28A
Processing a payment for a UN-designated terrorist entity
Refusing to apply s 26C basic expenses permits
No evidence that its customer and transaction screening manual was reviewed and approved after 2020
quiz.explanation: The notice cited the lack of evidence that the Screening of Customers and Transactions Manual had been reviewed and approved after 2020, among other s 42 findings. It did not report a designated-person payment.

sessions.title: Governance, Training, Records and Enforcement
sessions.summary: Prepare for a PA inspection: the board and compliance function under section 42A, ongoing training under section 43, record keeping under sections 22 to 24, and the section 45C sanctions toolkit with lessons from recent PA notices.
objectives: Describe the duties of the board and compliance function under s 42A
Design ongoing, role-based training that meets s 43
Apply the s 23 five-year record-keeping triggers and the s 24 third-party rules
Explain how the PA imposes administrative sanctions and how a bank can respond

cards.title: The inspection letter
cards.setting: Board risk committee, Kestrel Bank, Sandton. Tuesday, 4:00 pm.

lines.text: The PA's letter is here: an on-site FIC Act inspection under s 45B in six weeks. They want the RMCP, board minutes, training records and a sample of client files.
I want a straight answer. If they find gaps, is that a problem for management, or for this board?
For both. Section 42A puts the duty to ensure compliance on the board itself, and the PA has already sanctioned a bank specifically under s 42A.
And my branch training records are in three spreadsheets. Some tellers did the course in 2023 and nothing since.
Final stage. Governance, training, records and the sanctions toolkit. Then the boss level: the inspector's questions.

scenes.heading: The board (s 42A(1))
scenes.narration: The board of a bank that is a legal person must ensure that the bank and its employees comply with the FIC Act and the RMCP. It cannot delegate the duty away.

scenes.heading: The compliance function (s 42A(2))
scenes.narration: The bank must have a compliance function to help the board, and assign a person of sufficient competence and seniority to make that function effective.

scenes.heading: Ongoing training (s 43)
scenes.narration: The bank must give employees ongoing training so they can comply with the Act and the parts of the RMCP that apply to them. Failing to train is sanctionable under s 62.

scenes.heading: Records (ss 22 to 24)
scenes.narration: CDD and transaction records must be kept, for at least five years from the relevant event, and can be kept electronically or by a third party, but the bank stays liable.

scenes.heading: Sanctions (s 45C)
scenes.narration: If the PA finds non-compliance, it can caution, reprimand, direct remedial action, restrict business, or impose a financial penalty.

cards.title: Layers of accountability
cards.caption: Sections 61, 61B and 62 make failures at these layers non-compliance subject to administrative sanction.

items.label: Board of directors
items.detail: Ensures compliance with the Act and the RMCP; approves the RMCP (ss 42(2B), 42A(1)).

items.label: Senior management
items.detail: Implements the RMCP, approves higher-risk relationships such as foreign PEPs.

items.label: Compliance function
items.detail: Led by a competent, senior person; assists the board and oversees reporting (s 42A(2)).

items.label: Business lines and branches
items.detail: Apply CDD, monitoring and escalation every day.

items.label: Every employee
items.detail: Trained under s 43; personal duty to report suspicion under s 29.

cards.question: Which statement about the FIC Act and Kestrel's board is correct?
options: The board's role ends once it approves the RMCP
The board must ensure the bank and its employees comply, and can itself be found non-compliant
Only the compliance officer can be sanctioned for compliance failures
The board must personally file reports with the FIC
cards.explanation: Section 42A(1) places the duty to ensure compliance on the board, and s 61B makes a board or senior management that fails to do so non-compliant and subject to an administrative sanction.

cards.title: Records: what, how long, and where
cards.body:
**What to keep**
- **CDD records (s 22):** the information obtained under ss 21 to 21H, copies of or references to verification documents, and for relationships the nature, purpose and expected source of funds.
- **Transaction records (s 22A):** enough to reconstruct each transaction: amount and currency, date, parties, nature, business correspondence, and related account details.

**How long (s 23), at least five years from:**
- the date a business relationship **ends**;
- the date a transaction is **concluded**;
- the date a **s 29 report** was submitted, for records of the transaction or activity behind it.

**Where and how (s 24):** records may be kept **electronically**, if they can be reproduced legibly, or by a **third party**, if the bank has free and easy access and the records are readily available to the FIC and the PA. The bank must give the FIC and the PA the prescribed particulars of the third party, and it stays **liable** for the third party's failures.

cards.title: Five years from when?
cards.prompt: Under s 23, from which event does the five-year minimum run?

items.text: Copy of a closed client's identity verification documents
Source of funds information for a business relationship
Details of a once-off foreign exchange payment
Business correspondence about a specific transfer
Records of the activity that led to an STR filed last year
Documents behind a suspicious activity report on an attempted deposit

cards.title: Training that counts
cards.setting: Durban branch training room, Wednesday, 8:00 am.

lines.text: I've pulled the training records. Forty-two staff. Eleven last did AML training in 2023. Three new tellers haven't done any.
