Section 43 says 'ongoing'. A one-off course two years ago won't show the PA that staff can apply the current RMCP, including the 2022 changes.
Can we just get everyone to click through the e-learning by Friday?
Speed helps, but the inspector will ask what they learned and whether it matches their role. Let's design something we can defend.

cards.title: Fixing the training gap
cards.situation: With the inspection six weeks away, Kestrel finds that some branch staff have not been trained since 2023 and new tellers have had none. What is the best plan?

choices.text: Train new tellers before they handle transactions alone, refresh everyone on the current RMCP with role-specific content, test understanding, record completion, and set a recurring cycle
choices.outcome: Best. Section 43 requires ongoing training that enables staff to comply with the parts of the RMCP that apply to them. Role relevance, testing and records let the bank show this.

choices.text: Ask all staff to complete the same generic AML e-learning module by Friday
choices.outcome: Partly right: it closes the immediate gap, but a generic module may not cover the bank's own RMCP, the 2022 changes, or role-specific duties such as CTR and STR handling at the counter.

choices.text: Wait until after the inspection so the training can reflect the inspector's findings
choices.outcome: Poor. The duty to train exists now. Untrained staff handling transactions is a live s 43 gap and a s 62 exposure.

choices.text: Give each teller a copy of the RMCP and treat reading it as training
choices.outcome: Poor. Section 42(3) makes the RMCP available, but s 43 requires training that enables compliance. Handing over a document is not the same as building the skill.

cards.title: The PA's sanctions toolkit (s 45C(3))
cards.caption: Section 45C as inserted by Act 11 of 2008. The PA weighs the nature, duration, seriousness and extent of the breach, past record, remedial steps and other factors.

items.label: Caution
items.detail: A formal warning not to repeat the conduct. Used in every recent bank notice.

items.label: Reprimand
items.detail: A formal rebuke recorded against the institution.

items.label: Remedial directive or business restriction
items.detail: An order to fix specific failings, or a restriction or suspension of certain business activities.

items.label: Financial penalty
items.detail: Up to R50 million for a legal person or R10 million for a natural person; parts can be suspended on conditions.

cards.title: Real case: governance failure at State Bank of India, South Africa (PA, 2024)
cards.body:
The PA's **2 August 2024** notice on the **State Bank of India, South Africa** included a finding under **s 42A**: the bank failed to ensure compliance with ss 28, 29 and 42(2) of the FIC Act. That governance finding carried a caution and a **R1 million** penalty on its own.

The same notice found that the bank's risk assessment gave **no rationale** for the risk scores, mitigation decisions or controls, that its RMCP did not document the **governance structures** responsible for approving it and its amendments, and that its automated monitoring used **ineffective rules** with alerts closed late or without adequate reasons.

Total sanctions: four cautions and **R10 million**, with R4.5 million suspended for 36 months.

**Lesson:** when the controls fail, the PA also asks whether the board and senior management made sure they worked.

cards.title: Real case: records at HBZ and Standard Bank (PA, 2025)
cards.body:
Two 2025 notices show that record keeping is enforced on its own:
- **HBZ Bank (June 2025):** failed to keep records under **ss 22 and 23** for a high-risk **trade finance** client relationship, both active and terminated. The PA imposed a caution and a reprimand for that finding.
- **Standard Bank (January 2025):** failed under **s 23(c)** to keep a record of the **dates** on which 43 STRs or SARs were submitted to the FIC. The PA imposed a caution.

Why dates matter: the five-year period for records behind a report runs from the date it was submitted. Without that date, the bank cannot show when its retention period ends, or that the report was made on time.

**Lesson:** 'we did it' is not enough. The record has to prove what, when and by whom.

cards.title: How an administrative sanction is imposed
cards.prompt: Put the s 45B to s 45D process in order.
steps: The PA conducts an inspection of the bank under s 45B
The PA gives written notice of the alleged non-compliance and the intended sanction
The bank makes written representations within the period in the notice
The PA considers the representations and the s 45C(2) factors and decides
The PA notifies the bank of the decision, the reasons and the right to appeal
The bank may appeal to the Appeal Board under s 45D

cards.front: Who approved this RMCP, and when?
cards.back: Show board or senior management approval under s 42(2B) and the date of the last review under s 42(2C).
Name the person assigned under s 42A(2)(b) and show their competence and seniority.

cards.front: How do you know staff can apply the RMCP?
cards.back: Show role-based s 43 training records, content, test results and refresh dates.
Show the s 23(c) record of the submission date and the supporting records.

cards.front: Can the PA see records held by your vendor?
cards.back: Yes: under s 24 the bank must have free and easy access, and remains liable for the vendor.

cards.front: What happens if a penalty is suspended?
cards.back: Under s 45C(4)(c), part of a sanction can be suspended on conditions for up to five years.

cards.question: Under s 45C(4)(b), what extra step can the PA take when imposing a financial penalty on a bank?
options: Require the bank's auditors to pay the penalty
Direct that the penalty be paid by the natural persons personally responsible for the non-compliance
Transfer the penalty to the client who was harmed
Convert the penalty into a criminal fine
cards.explanation: Section 45C(4)(b) allows the Centre or supervisory body to direct that a financial penalty be paid by natural persons for whose actions the institution is accountable, if they were personally responsible.

cards.title: Stage 5 take-aways
items: The board must ensure compliance (s 42A(1)); the bank needs a compliance function led by a competent, senior person (s 42A(2)).
Training must be ongoing and enable each employee to apply the RMCP parts relevant to them (s 43); failure is sanctionable (s 62).
Keep CDD and transaction records for at least five years from the end of the relationship, the transaction, or the report submission (ss 22-23).
Records may be electronic or held by a third party, but the bank stays liable and must give access (s 24).
Section 45C sanctions: caution, reprimand, directive, restriction, and penalties up to R50 million for a legal person, with appeal under s 45D.
Recent PA notices against Standard Bank, Capitec, SBI, HBZ and Bank of Taiwan show inspections test evidence, not intentions.

cards.prompt: If the PA inspected your area tomorrow, which single piece of evidence (an approval, a training record, a report date) would you struggle to produce? What will you do about it this week?

quiz.question: Under s 42A(2), what must a bank that is a legal person have to support its board?
options: An external AML auditor appointed by the Prudential Authority
A separate AML board committee chaired by an independent director
A compliance function, with a person of sufficient competence and seniority assigned to make it effective
A money laundering reporting officer registered with the FIC
quiz.explanation: Section 42A(2) requires a compliance function and the assignment of a person with sufficient competence and seniority. The Act does not prescribe the other structures.

quiz.question: Which provision makes a board that fails to ensure compliance under s 42A(1) non-compliant and subject to an administrative sanction?
options: Section 61B
Section 45D
Section 29(4)
Section 21H
quiz.explanation: Section 61B, inserted in 2017, applies to a board or senior management that fails to ensure compliance under s 42A(1), and to a bank that fails to appoint the person required by s 42A(2).

quiz.question: What does s 43 require of a bank regarding training?
options: A one-time induction course for staff who open accounts
Ongoing training so employees can comply with the Act and the parts of the RMCP that apply to them
Annual training for the compliance function only
Training approved in advance by the FIC for each staff category
quiz.explanation: The 2017 substitution of s 43 requires ongoing training enabling employees to comply with the Act and the applicable parts of the RMCP. The Act itself does not fix a frequency or require FIC approval.

quiz.question: A business relationship with a client ended on 30 June 2024. Until at least when must Kestrel keep the CDD records?
options: 30 June 2027
31 December 2024
30 June 2034
30 June 2029
quiz.explanation: Section 23(a) requires records about the business relationship to be kept for at least five years from the date the relationship ends.

quiz.question: Kestrel stores transaction records with a cloud vendor that loses part of the archive. Who is liable to the PA for the gap?
options: Kestrel, because s 24 keeps the bank liable for a third party's failure
The vendor alone, because it held the records
Nobody, if the vendor contract excluded liability
The FIC, because it approved the vendor
quiz.explanation: Section 24(2) makes the accountable institution liable when a third party fails to keep records properly on its behalf.

quiz.question: Which list correctly states sanctions available under s 45C(3)?
options: Caution, licence cancellation, imprisonment, financial penalty
Reprimand, deregistration as a bank, client compensation order
Caution, reprimand, remedial directive, restriction or suspension of business activities, financial penalty
Warning letter, public apology, criminal fine, director disqualification
quiz.explanation: Section 45C(3) lists caution, reprimand, a directive to take remedial action, restriction or suspension of specified business activities, and a financial penalty.

quiz.question: What is the maximum financial penalty under s 45C(3)(e) for a legal person such as a bank?
options: R10 million
R13 million
R100 million
R50 million
quiz.explanation: Section 45C(3)(e) caps the penalty at R50 million for a legal person and R10 million for a natural person. R13 million was Standard Bank's 2025 total, not a cap.

quiz.question: The PA found in 2024 that the State Bank of India, South Africa had failed to ensure compliance with ss 28, 29 and 42(2). Under which governance provision was this finding made?
options: Section 26C
Section 42A
Section 21B
Section 34
quiz.explanation: The August 2024 notice cited s 42A for failing to ensure compliance with ss 28, 29 and 42(2), with a caution and a R1 million penalty.

quiz.question: Why did the Standard Bank s 23(c) finding about missing STR submission dates matter?
options: Because STR dates must be published in the bank's annual report
Because the FIC deletes reports after five years without the date
The retention period for records behind a report runs from the date it was submitted
Because the client is entitled to know when a report was made
quiz.explanation: Section 23(c) runs the five-year period from the date a s 29 report was submitted. Without that record the bank cannot prove timeliness or retention. Disclosing reports to clients is prohibited.

quiz.question: Before imposing an administrative sanction, what must the PA give the bank under s 45C(5)?
options: Written notice of the alleged breach and intended sanction, and a chance to make representations
A copy of every other bank's inspection report for comparison
An oral hearing before a High Court judge
Thirty days to fix the problem, after which no sanction may follow
quiz.explanation: Section 45C(5) requires reasonable written notice of the alleged non-compliance, the intended sanction and its particulars, and the right to make written representations.

references.title: Financial Intelligence Centre Amendment Act 1 of 2017 (Government Gazette 40821)
references.provision: Section 43 (training) and section 62 (failure to provide training), as substituted by ss 29 and 48
references.note: Substituted s 43: an accountable institution must give its employees ongoing training so they can comply with the Act and with the parts of the Risk Management and Compliance Programme that apply to them; s 62 (as substituted) makes failure to train a non-compliance subject to administrative sanction.

references.title: Financial Intelligence Centre Amendment Act 1 of 2017 (Government Gazette 40821)
references.provision: Sections 42(1)-(4), 42A, 61 and 61B (RMCP, governance and related sanctions)
references.note: Banks must develop, document, maintain, implement, approve and regularly review an RMCP available to staff; the board must ensure compliance, supported by a compliance function led by a competent, senior person.

references.title: Financial Intelligence Centre Amendment Act 1 of 2017 (Government Gazette 40821)
references.provision: Sections 20A-21H (customer due diligence, beneficial ownership, PEPs) and 22-24 (records)
references.note: Sets the CDD, beneficial ownership, ongoing due diligence and PEP measures, and requires CDD and transaction records to be kept for at least five years from the relevant event.

references.title: Financial Intelligence Centre Amendment Act 1 of 2017 (Government Gazette 40821)
references.provision: Sections 26A-26C and 28A (as inserted or amended by ss 17 and 20), 29 (as amended by s 21) and 34
references.note: Creates the UN financial sanctions regime, reporting of designated persons' property, the s 26B ground for suspicious reports and the FIC's power to pause transactions for up to 10 days.

references.title: General Laws (Anti-Money Laundering and Combating Terrorism Financing) Amendment Act 22 of 2022 (Government Gazette 47815)
references.provision: Sections 18, 22-29, 39, 40 and 51-53 (amending FIC Act ss 1, 21B-21H, 26A-26C, 42, 49A and Schedules 3A-3C)
references.note: Adds proliferation financing to the RMCP, revises the beneficial owner definition, renames PEP categories and adds prominent influential persons, gives UN listings immediate effect and makes s 26B breaches sanctionable.

references.title: Protection of Constitutional Democracy against Terrorist and Related Activities Amendment Act 23 of 2022 (Government Gazette 47803)
references.provision: Sections 20-21 (repeal of POCDATARA ss 25-26) and the Schedule (FIC Act ss 26A and 28A)
references.note: Repeals the presidential proclamation route and moves UN terrorism designations onto the FIC Act s 26A mechanism, keeping earlier proclamations valid.

references.title: Financial Intelligence Centre Act 38 of 2001 (Government Gazette 22886)
references.provision: Sections 28 and 29 (cash threshold and suspicious and unusual transaction reports)
references.note: Requires reports of cash above the prescribed amount and of knowledge or suspicion by anyone carrying on, managing or employed by a business, and prohibits tipping off.

references.title: Financial Intelligence Centre Amendment Act 11 of 2008
references.note: Lists the sanctions (caution, reprimand, directive, restriction, penalty up to R10 million for natural persons and R50 million for legal persons), the factors to weigh, suspension for up to five years and the notice-and-representations process.

references.title: Amendments to Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing Control Regulations, 2002 (Government Notice 2638, Government Gazette 47302)
references.note: Sets the cash threshold reporting amount at R49,999.99 and requires a cash threshold report no later than 3 days after awareness, no longer referring to a series of cash transactions.

references.title: Anti-Money Laundering and Countering the Financing of Terrorism (AML/CFT)
references.note: Explains the PA's risk-based FIC Act supervision of banks, the s 45C sanction factors, and that the PA does not formally approve RMCPs.

references.title: Treasury on South Africa exiting FATF greylist on 24 October 2025
references.note: Confirms the grey-list exit after listing in February 2023 and a 22-item action plan, and expects the next mutual evaluation to run from 2026 to October 2027.

references.title: Prudential Authority imposes administrative sanctions on The Standard Bank of South Africa Limited (media release, 24 January 2025)
references.provision: Findings under ss 21C, 23(c), 28, 29 and FIC Directive 5 of 2019
references.note: Six cautions and R13 million in penalties; cites the 48-hour alert expectation and the 15-day reporting period in regulation 24(3).

bank.question: Kestrel launches a new instant cross-border payment app. Under s 42(2)(a) as amended in 2022, what must the RMCP enable the bank to do about it?
options: Register the app with the FIC before any client may use it
Identify, assess, monitor, mitigate and manage the ML, TF and PF risk of new and existing products
Apply simplified due diligence until the first suspicious report is filed
Seek the Prudential Authority's written approval of the product's risk rating
bank.explanation: The 2022 amendment made s 42(2)(a) refer to 'new and existing products or services' and to proliferation financing. The duty is to assess and manage risk, not to obtain product approval.

bank.question: An inspector asks Kestrel why its RMCP says nothing about foreign branches. Kestrel has none. What should the RMCP have contained?
options: Nothing, because the FIC Act does not apply to banks without foreign operations
A copy of a template foreign-branch policy in case the bank expands later
A PA exemption letter covering the omitted paragraph
A statement that the foreign-operations paragraph does not apply and why
bank.explanation: Section 42(2A) requires the RMCP to indicate any s 42(2) paragraph that is not applicable and the reason. Silence is a gap; a PA exemption is not part of the scheme.

bank.question: Which statement about the Prudential Authority's role in a bank's RMCP is accurate?
options: It assesses the adequacy and effectiveness of the RMCP but does not formally approve it
It approves each RMCP and any material amendment before use
It writes a standard RMCP that every bank must adopt
It has no role, because the FIC alone supervises RMCPs
bank.explanation: The PA's published guidance says it assesses ML/TF risk management and compliance programmes and that there is no requirement for it to formally approve a bank's RMCP.

bank.question: Kestrel's executive committee changed the RMCP's EDD triggers in March, but the board has not yet seen the change. A PA inspector asks for evidence of approval. Which real sanction shows the risk?
options: HBZ Bank, which was sanctioned for failing to report cash over the threshold
Standard Bank, which was sanctioned for operating without any RMCP
Bank of Taiwan, South Africa Branch, which could not evidence approval of RMCP amendments before implementation
State Bank of India, which was sanctioned for processing a sanctioned payment
bank.explanation: The June 2025 notice on the Bank of Taiwan, South Africa Branch cited the lack of evidence that material RMCP amendments were approved before implementation. The other options misdescribe those cases.

bank.question: A bank's RMCP documentation is kept in a locked compliance folder. A teller has never seen it. Which provisions make this a problem?
options: Section 26B, because RMCP documents are restricted property
Section 29(3), because the RMCP contains report details
Section 42(3) on availability to employees and s 61, which makes that failure sanctionable
Section 21E, because the teller cannot complete CDD
bank.explanation: Section 42(3) requires RMCP documentation to be available to each employee involved in covered transactions, and s 61(b) makes failure to do so non-compliance subject to sanction.

bank.question: According to National Treasury, when is South Africa's next FATF mutual evaluation expected to conclude?
options: October 2027
October 2025
February 2026
December 2030
bank.explanation: Treasury's 24 October 2025 statement said the next mutual evaluation is expected to start in the first half of 2026 and conclude in October 2027.

bank.question: Which development is correctly matched to the Act that introduced it?
options: The Risk Management and Compliance Programme: the original FIC Act of 2001
Proliferation financing in the RMCP: the FIC Amendment Act of 2017
Section 42A board governance duties: the General Laws Amendment Act of 2022
Administrative sanctions under s 45C: the FIC Amendment Act 11 of 2008
bank.explanation: Section 45C was inserted by Act 11 of 2008. The RMCP and s 42A came with the 2017 amendments, and proliferation financing with the 2022 General Laws amendments.

bank.question: HBZ Bank's RMCP said trade finance was 'medium' risk, but the bank could not show why. Which part of a risk-based approach failed most clearly?
options: Reporting: the bank did not file cash threshold reports
Assessment: the inherent risk rating lacked a documented rationale
Sanctions: the bank failed to screen against UN lists
Training: the bank had not trained branch tellers
bank.explanation: The June 2025 notice cited the absence of a documented rationale for the medium rating and of a confirmed residual rating, which goes to how risk was assessed under s 42(2)(a).

bank.question: Sipho argues that because South Africa left the grey list, Kestrel can relax its RMCP reviews. Which response best reflects both the law and the national context?
options: Section 42(2C) still requires regular review, and the coming mutual evaluation will test effectiveness
He is right, because review duties applied only during increased monitoring
He is right, provided the board signs a waiver for the next two years
He is wrong only because the PA has issued a directive extending the grey list
bank.explanation: Regular review is a standing s 42(2C) duty, not a grey-list measure, and Treasury warned that effectiveness will be tested in the next mutual evaluation.

bank.question: A company's shares are spread among 40 small shareholders, none with control. A family member who holds no shares runs it through a shareholder agreement giving veto rights. Who is the beneficial owner under s 21B(2)?
options: Nobody, because no shareholder holds a controlling interest
Each of the 40 shareholders, because together they own the company
The family member, as a person exercising control of the company through other means
The company secretary, because the secretary keeps the share register
bank.explanation: If no natural person has a controlling ownership interest, s 21B(2)(a)(ii) moves to persons who control the company through other means, such as veto rights.

bank.question: A trust deed does not name beneficiaries but describes them as 'the descendants of the founder'. What must Kestrel establish under s 21B(4)(e)?
options: The identity of every living descendant, verified with identity documents
The particulars of how the beneficiaries are determined, with reasonable steps to verify them
Nothing about beneficiaries, because none is named
The beneficiaries' tax numbers, obtained from SARS
bank.explanation: Where beneficiaries are not named, s 21B(4)(e)(ii) requires the particulars of how they are determined, and s 21B(4)(f) requires reasonable steps to verify those particulars.

bank.question: One trustee of a client trust is a company. What did the 2022 amendments add to the bank's duties?
options: Replacing the corporate trustee with a natural person
Obtaining the Master of the High Court's consent to open the account
Treating the trust as a high-risk client by default
Identifying the beneficial owner of that corporate trustee
bank.explanation: Section 21B(4)(d)(iA), added in 2022, requires the bank to identify the beneficial owner of a trustee that is a legal person or acts for a partnership.

bank.question: A domestic PEP's relationship is rated higher risk under Kestrel's RMCP. Which set of measures does s 21G require?
options: Board approval, a police clearance certificate and monthly account statements to the FIC
A cash threshold report on every deposit and a ban on cash withdrawals
Notification to the Prudential Authority and a 30-day cooling-off period
Senior management approval, reasonable measures on source of wealth and funds, and enhanced ongoing monitoring
bank.explanation: Section 21G mirrors s 21F once the relationship is assessed as higher risk: senior management approval, source of wealth and funds measures, and enhanced ongoing monitoring.

bank.question: Under the 2017 wording, a domestic official stopped being covered 12 months after leaving office. What is the position after the 2022 amendments to Schedule 3A?
options: The cut-off was extended to 24 months for all domestic officials
The 12-month cut-off was removed: a person who has held the function remains a domestic PEP
The cut-off still applies, but only to judges and military officers
Domestic PEPs were abolished and replaced by prominent influential persons
bank.explanation: The 2022 amendments reworded Schedule 3A to 'holds ... or has held' a prominent public function, dropping the 12-month limit. Prominent influential persons became a separate Schedule 3C category.

bank.question: A CFO left a company supplying a government department above the Minister's value 18 months ago. Is she a prominent influential person under Schedule 3C?
options: Yes, because PIP status, like PEP status, no longer lapses
No, because Schedule 3C covers the position held now or in the preceding 12 months
Yes, but only if she now works for another state supplier
No, because CFOs are not listed in Schedule 3C
bank.explanation: Schedule 3C covers a person who holds, or has held at any time in the preceding 12 months, the listed company roles. CFOs are listed. The 12-month window survives for PIPs.

bank.question: Kestrel cannot obtain information on a prospective client's source of funds, and the client refuses to explain. Which outcome does the Act require?
options: Opening the account with a lower transaction limit
Opening the account and asking again at the first annual review
Referring the client to the PA for a source of funds ruling
Not establishing the relationship, and considering a s 29 report
bank.explanation: Source of funds is s 21A information. Section 21E bars establishing the relationship if it cannot be obtained, and tells the bank to consider reporting.

bank.question: Capitec's 2024 sanction covered CDD gaps in both retail and business banking. What was the combined CDD penalty for the two segments before suspensions?
options: R35 million
R56.25 million
R13 million
R20 million
bank.explanation: The notice imposed R20 million (retail) and R15 million (business banking) for the CDD findings, R35 million in total. R56.25 million was the overall sanction across all findings.

bank.question: Which pair of people is included in 'immediate family member' under s 21H(2)?
options: A cousin, and a grandparent
A business partner, and a former employee
A previous spouse, and a step-sibling's life partner
A nephew, and a godparent
bank.explanation: Section 21H(2) lists spouses, civil or life partners (and previous ones), children and step-children and their partners, parents, and siblings and step-siblings and their partners.

bank.question: A client withdraws R52,000 in cash to buy livestock at an auction. Documents match and nothing is unusual. Which report applies?
options: A suspicious report under s 29 because the amount is large
No report, because CTRs cover deposits only
A cash threshold report under s 28, with no suspicious report needed
A s 28A report because livestock auctions are high risk
bank.explanation: Section 28 covers cash paid by the bank to the client as well as cash received, above R49,999.99. Size alone is not a s 29 ground.

bank.question: Which change did Government Notice 2638 of 2022 make to regulation 24(4)?
options: It extended the CTR deadline from 2 to 3 days and removed the reference to a series of cash transactions
It shortened the STR deadline from 15 days to 3 days
It introduced a 48-hour deadline for attending to monitoring alerts
It raised the CTR threshold to R99,999.99 for business clients
bank.explanation: GN 2638 substituted '3' for '2' days and deleted 'or series of cash transactions' from regulation 24(4). The threshold change (to R49,999.99) was in regulation 22B.

bank.question: A teller notices a client splitting R140,000 into three cash deposits of under R49,999.99 at different branches on the same day. Which statement is correct?
options: No report is due because each deposit is under the threshold
A CTR is due for the total because deposits on one day are always combined
The teller must refuse the deposits and tell the client why
The pattern suggests avoiding a reporting duty, which is a s 29 ground, so it should be escalated for an STR
bank.explanation: Conducting transactions to avoid a reporting duty is a s 29(1)(b)(iii) ground. Telling the client why risks tipping off.

bank.question: Under FIC Directive 5 of 2019, as applied in PA sanction notices, how quickly should automated monitoring alerts be attended to?
options: Within 15 days
Within 48 hours
Within 3 days
Within 30 days
bank.explanation: The PA's notices on Standard Bank and Capitec cited failures to attend to automated alerts within the 48 hours required by Directive 5 of 2019. Fifteen days relates to the STR period and three days to CTRs.

bank.question: The FIC directs Kestrel under s 34 not to proceed with a transfer. The direction is issued on a Thursday before a long weekend. How is the maximum period counted?
options: Up to 10 days, excluding Saturdays, Sundays and public holidays
Ten calendar days from the direction, including the weekend
Five business days, as under the original Act
Until the client consents to the release
bank.explanation: The 2017 amendment set the maximum at 10 days and s 34(2) excludes Saturdays, Sundays and proclaimed public holidays. Five days was the pre-2017 limit.

bank.question: A relationship manager tells a client, 'I'm not allowed to say we reported you, but you'd better be careful.' Which provision has most likely been breached?
options: Section 21C(2), which requires continuing CDD after a report
Section 28, which governs cash threshold reports
Section 29(4), which bars disclosing knowledge or suspicion that a report was or will be made
Section 42A, which governs the board's duty
bank.explanation: Section 29(3) and (4) prohibit disclosing that a report has been or will be made, or its contents. A hint that signals a report still discloses it.

bank.question: What did the 2022 amendment to s 21D add?
options: A duty to close any account on which a s 29 report has been filed
A duty to repeat identification and verification steps, as needed, after making a s 29 report
A ban on any further CDD once a report is made
A duty to inform the client that their information will be re-verified because of a report
bank.explanation: Section 21D as substituted in 2022 applies when the bank doubts earlier information or makes a s 29 report, requiring it to repeat ss 21 and 21B steps to the extent necessary.

bank.question: Standard Bank's 2025 notice found 94,558 alerts closed beyond the 15-day reporting period. Why was that treated as a reporting failure, not just a backlog?
options: Because each closed alert must be filed as a separate CTR
Because the FIC requires a report on every alert regardless of outcome
Because closed alerts must be deleted within 15 days under POPIA
Alerts that lead to reports must be resolved in time for the report to meet the regulation 24(3) period
bank.explanation: If alert review runs past the 15-day period, any resulting STR is late. The PA linked Directive 5 alert handling to the regulation 24(3) period.

bank.question: Which institution and person must report under s 29?
options: Only the bank's compliance officer, on behalf of the bank
Only accountable institutions registered with the FIC, through their board
Only persons who have personal proof of a crime
Any person who carries on, manages or is employed by a business and knows or suspects one of the listed matters
bank.explanation: Section 29(1) applies to anyone who carries on a business, is in charge of or manages one, or is employed by one, and knows or suspects. Proof is not needed.

bank.question: A UN Security Council committee adds an entity to a Chapter VII sanctions list at 3 pm New York time. A payment to it reaches Kestrel at 9 am the next day, before any FIC notice. What should Kestrel do?
options: Process it because the FIC Director has not yet published a notice
Treat the designation as already effective and stop the payment, reporting as required
Process it but file a s 29 report afterwards
Ask the client to confirm in writing that it does not know the entity
bank.explanation: Since 2022, s 26A(1) gives a Chapter VII resolution immediate effect upon adoption, so the s 26B prohibitions already apply. The Director's notice follows.

bank.question: Which of these may the Minister permit under s 26C as a dealing with a designated person's property?
options: Investment of the frozen funds in higher-yielding products
A payment due under a contract made before the person was designated, as long as the person does not receive it
Transfer of the funds to a relative who is not designated
Payment of a new loan taken out after designation
bank.explanation: Section 26C(2) lists basic expenses, earlier judgments, pre-designation contractual payments to third parties, accruing interest, and certain payments due to the designated person under prior obligations if not received by them.

bank.question: After a new s 26A notice, Kestrel finds an existing client match. Which provision requires the report of the property to the FIC?
options: Section 28
Section 26C
Section 45B
Section 28A(1)
bank.explanation: Section 28A(1) requires an accountable institution with property owned or controlled by or for a designated person to report that fact and the prescribed particulars to the FIC within the prescribed period.

bank.question: Before 2022, terrorist entities named by the President under POCDATARA s 25 were handled separately. What happens to those earlier proclamations now?
options: They remain valid and have the same effect as a notice under FIC Act s 26A(3)
They lapsed on 29 December 2022 and must be re-issued
They are now administered by the Prudential Authority
They apply only to persons who were South African residents
bank.explanation: Section 27(1A) of POCDATARA, inserted in 2022, keeps earlier proclamations valid with the same force as a s 26A(3) notice.

bank.question: A client's payment is for 'industrial equipment' to a newly formed trading company abroad. The end user is unclear, the price is far above market, and goods are routed through several hubs. No party is designated. What is the best response?
options: Process it, because sanctions apply only to designated persons
Reject it automatically and close the client's account
Escalate it as a possible proliferation financing concern and consider a s 29 report
Ask the client to obtain a s 26C permission from the Minister
bank.explanation: Proliferation financing risk extends beyond list matches. The RMCP must cover PF risk, and an unexplained pattern of this kind may be a s 29 suspicion. Section 26C does not apply where nobody is designated.

bank.question: Which statement about who the s 26B prohibitions apply to is correct?
options: They apply only to banks and their employees
They apply only to institutions supervised by the PA
They apply to any person, not only accountable institutions
They apply only to persons resident in South Africa who know of the listing
bank.explanation: Section 26B begins 'No person may', so the prohibitions apply generally. Section 49A(2) makes accountable institutions and other persons who fail to comply subject to administrative sanction.

bank.question: Why did the 2022 amendments matter for a bank that already screened against UN lists?
options: UN listings now take effect on adoption, so lists must be updated quickly to avoid breaches before notices appear
Banks no longer need to screen because the FIC now freezes funds directly
UN listings now take effect only after a PA directive, slowing updates
Screening is now required only for cross-border payments
bank.explanation: Immediate effect on adoption means any delay in updating screening lists creates exposure under s 26B before the Director's notice is even published.

bank.question: Which element is part of the FIC Act definition of proliferation financing?
options: Any payment to a State-owned defence company in another country
Any transaction in goods listed under South African export controls
Funding of a terrorist act involving conventional weapons
Support to a non-State actor that may be used to finance weapons of mass destruction or their means of delivery
bank.explanation: The 2022 definition refers to property, services or economic support to a non-State actor that may finance nuclear, chemical or biological weapons and their means of delivery.

bank.question: Kestrel's board minutes show the board noted the RMCP but never discussed compliance reports for two years. Which provision is most at risk?
options: Section 26A(3), the Director's duty to publish notices
Section 42A(1), the board's duty to ensure compliance with the Act and the RMCP
Section 28, the cash threshold reporting duty
Section 21H, the PEP family member rule
bank.explanation: Section 42A(1) places the duty to ensure compliance on the board. Noting the RMCP without overseeing whether it works is weak evidence of that duty, and s 61B makes failure sanctionable.

bank.question: Who must Kestrel assign to make its compliance function effective under s 42A(2)(b)?
options: A person with sufficient competence and seniority
A person registered as an attorney or chartered accountant
A non-executive director with no operational role
An external consultant approved by the FIC
bank.explanation: Section 42A(2)(b) requires a person of sufficient competence and seniority. The Act does not require a professional qualification, a director or an FIC-approved consultant.

bank.question: Kestrel trained all staff in 2022 but not since. The RMCP has changed twice. What is the most accurate assessment?
options: It is compliant, because the Act sets no training frequency
It is compliant until the next PA inspection identifies a gap
It is exposed under ss 43 and 62, because training must be ongoing and match the current RMCP
It is exposed only if a staff member has missed an STR
bank.explanation: Section 43 requires ongoing training so staff can comply with the RMCP as it applies to them. Training that predates two RMCP changes does not achieve that, and s 62 makes failure sanctionable.

bank.question: A once-off foreign exchange transaction was concluded on 15 March 2023, and an STR on it was submitted on 2 April 2023. Until when must the transaction-related records be kept, at minimum?
options: Until 15 March 2028 only, because the transaction rule always prevails
Until at least 2 April 2028, because the records behind the report run from its submission date
Until 31 December 2023, because once-off transactions are short-term
Until 2 April 2033, because reports double the period
bank.explanation: Section 23(b) runs five years from the transaction and s 23(c) five years from the report submission. Keeping records to 2 April 2028 satisfies both.

bank.question: Which statement about the PA's power to suspend part of an administrative sanction is correct?
options: It may suspend a penalty only if the bank pays it within 30 days
It may not suspend financial penalties, only cautions
It may suspend a sanction indefinitely if the bank cooperates
It may suspend any part on conditions for up to five years
bank.explanation: Section 45C(4)(c) allows suspension of any part of a sanction on conditions for a period not exceeding five years. Recent notices used 24- and 36-month suspensions.

bank.question: Which factor must the PA consider under s 45C(2) when choosing a sanction?
options: The institution's share price on the day of the decision
The number of clients the institution has in rural areas
Whether the institution's auditors agreed with the finding
Remedial steps the institution has taken to prevent a recurrence
bank.explanation: Section 45C(2) lists the nature, duration, seriousness and extent of the breach, previous non-compliance, remedial steps, steps by other supervisors or associations, and other relevant factors.

bank.question: Every one of the recent PA notices on Standard Bank, Capitec, HBZ, SBI and Bank of Taiwan ended with a similar statement. What was it?
options: The bank had been found to have laundered money for clients
The bank cooperated and had taken remedial action to address the deficiencies
The bank had lost its licence pending a court review
The bank's directors had been personally fined
bank.explanation: Each notice recorded cooperation and remedial action. The SBI notice also stated the sanctions were not due to involvement in laundering or terrorist financing.

bank.question: If Kestrel disagrees with a PA sanction, what route does the FIC Act provide?
options: An application to the FIC to reverse the PA's decision
An appeal to the Appeal Board under s 45D
A complaint to the Banking Ombud
A request to the Minister to cancel the penalty under s 26C
bank.explanation: The PA must notify the bank of its right to appeal under s 45D, which provides for appeals against decisions of the Centre or a supervisory body.
